messages.author: b77c540835bb3b48
messages.subject: Async / non-blocking reactives in Shiny
parts:
Hi Shiny Users,

I was recently wondering about the potential approaches to circumvent the synchronous nature of R / Shiny, in particular that a long-running R calculation will block the whole user interface. My first intuition is that spawning separate R processes is the only way to go. 

Using the 'future' package I have come up with an asynchronous drop-in replacement to eventReactive, which requires no code change compared to the usual eventReactive and can achieve asynchronous (non-blocking) evaluation. A small gist is available here: https://gist.github.com/andrewsali/3317e5954459fef2f5fed68d68c1ac92 

The reason for using the 'future' package is that it takes care of spawning the new R process and automatically exporting the relevant variables by static code inspection of the handler expression.

However this approach also has a few small drawbacks: 1) it's not possible to have side-effects in the handler expression, 2) The reactive produced by my async version will not invalidate downstream when the calculation starts, but instead when the calculation finishes and the value is returned. This means that the 'recalculating' class (opacity) is not applied to an output depending on the async reactive whilst the calculation is running.

The reason why I thought to make eventReactive async is that the event expression (usually the fast part) can remain synchronous and the long-running handler expression can be sent for async evaluation. Also, by creating an async version of a 'reactive' it's relatively a minor issue that side-effects are not allowed for in the handler expression.

I would be very curious to know what others have been doing to have async / non-blocking behaviour in Shiny. Also, as far as I know there is an 'async' version of Shiny being worked on, I would be interested if there is some information on what the underlying approach taken is.

Cheers,

Andras

messages.author: b77c540835bb3b48
messages.subject: Re: Async / non-blocking reactives in Shiny
parts:
The eventReactiveAsync() function is very short in my gist, so you should be able to adapt it quickly to your needs. Although I think you can use it out of the box without modifications as well.

The setup is fairly simple (and not too original): 
  1. start a 'multiprocess' future (i.e. on *nix based system do a fork of the process, on Windows start a new process). The future package will export the relevant objects to the new process by examining the handler expression.
  2. set up an observer that checks if the results are ready via 'future::resolved()' (note the 'd' at the end, this is a non-blocking check) 
  3. if results are ready invalidate with the calculated value the reactive that is produced by the eventReactiveAsync() function.
I am not sure what the advantage is of the 'callr' package mentioned by Dean compared to 'future', as it also starts a new R process. What is nice about 'future' on the other hand is the automatic variable exporting based on the expression to be evaluated.

Cheers,

Andras

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Async / non-blocking reactives in Shiny
parts:
The eventReactiveAsync approach is pretty similar to what I did in the gist that Dean referred to. Andras describes it well. Kudos for figuring out this solution. My gist solution differs in that it uses mcparallel instead of futures, but they're used in almost exactly the same way. Also my solution deals with errors thrown during the task, by propagating them to the reactive expressions; I don't see that in your solution right now but you obviously could add that easily. Anyway, these solutions clearly belong in the same category.

The "proper" async support that's coming will be quite different. I don't have any documentation that I'm comfortable sharing right at this moment--they will probably cause more confusion than clarity at this point. But I will say that the goal is to work with both callr and futures (and no, you won't be able to execute async R code without forking, though you can execute async C/C++ code without forking). It doesn't use the "req(FALSE) until the result is ready" approach; instead, it's much more like JavaScript promises, but with 1) a pipeable syntax that's much friendlier to R users, and 2) a novel(?) extensibility point that allows Shiny reactivity to integrate cleanly.

I should have much more to talk about later this summer.

That said, nothing I'm working on should affect your solution--if it's working well for you, I don't see anything wrong with it (other than, it'd be good to propagate errors).

Thanks very much Joe for outlining what direction the async developments are taking!

Whilst eventReactiveAsync works OK in most of the cases (as well pointed out, error handling should be added), a big limitation is that it doesn't integrate nicely with Shiny JS events (an output depending on the async reactive is not in a 'recalculating' state during the async execution). Thus automatic loading notifiers such as shinycssloaders will also not work out-of-the box for outputs that depend on eventReactiveAsync. 

Given these limitations, a 'proper' async integration into Shiny will be really great, I am very much looking forward to developments in this area.

On Sunday, 11 June 2017 06:58:12 UTC-4, Andrew Sali wrote:
Hi Shiny Users,

I was recently wondering about the potential approaches to circumvent the synchronous nature of R / Shiny, in particular that a long-running R calculation will block the whole user interface. My first intuition is that spawning separate R processes is the only way to go. 

Using the 'future' package I have come up with an asynchronous drop-in replacement to eventReactive, which requires no code change compared to the usual eventReactive and can achieve asynchronous (non-blocking) evaluation. A small gist is available here: https://gist.github.com/andrewsali/3317e5954459fef2f5fed68d68c1ac92 

The reason for using the 'future' package is that it takes care of spawning the new R process and automatically exporting the relevant variables by static code inspection of the handler expression.

However this approach also has a few small drawbacks: 1) it's not possible to have side-effects in the handler expression, 2) The reactive produced by my async version will not invalidate downstream when the calculation starts, but instead when the calculation finishes and the value is returned. This means that the 'recalculating' class (opacity) is not applied to an output depending on the async reactive whilst the calculation is running.

The reason why I thought to make eventReactive async is that the event expression (usually the fast part) can remain synchronous and the long-running handler expression can be sent for async evaluation. Also, by creating an async version of a 'reactive' it's relatively a minor issue that side-effects are not allowed for in the handler expression.

I would be very curious to know what others have been doing to have async / non-blocking behaviour in Shiny. Also, as far as I know there is an 'async' version of Shiny being worked on, I would be interested if there is some information on what the underlying approach taken is.

Cheers,

Andras

The eventReactiveAsync() function is very short in my gist, so you should be able to adapt it quickly to your needs. Although I think you can use it out of the box without modifications as well.

The setup is fairly simple (and not too original): 
  1. start a 'multiprocess' future (i.e. on *nix based system do a fork of the process, on Windows start a new process). The future package will export the relevant objects to the new process by examining the handler expression.
  2. set up an observer that checks if the results are ready via 'future::resolved()' (note the 'd' at the end, this is a non-blocking check) 
  3. if results are ready invalidate with the calculated value the reactive that is produced by the eventReactiveAsync() function.
I am not sure what the advantage is of the 'callr' package mentioned by Dean compared to 'future', as it also starts a new R process. What is nice about 'future' on the other hand is the automatic variable exporting based on the expression to be evaluated.

Cheers,

Andras

parts:
dear Andrew,
    After migrate your code into my project, there's still blocked problem(verbatinTextOutput becomes blocked after calling importFile()) if it tooks too long(about 2 minutes). 
My project uses fileInput to upload excel files, and verbatinTextOutput to display calculate result text.
I write importFile() function in common.R(uses openxlsx to read excel .xlsx files and validate some column and append errors to data.table), and load it in the very begining of server.R
    Besides I uses André le Blond 's future solution, still have the blocking problem(reference site https://stackoverflow.com/questions/41610354/calling-a-shiny-javascript-callback-from-within-a-future)
Attach my partial code as belowings~

getFileInput <- eventReactiveAsync(input$fileInput,{
    Sys.sleep(1)
    input$fileInput
  })
  
  importAndValidate <- function(iFileInput) {
   if (is.null(iFileInput))
      return (NULL)
    # Create a Progress object
    progress <- shiny::Progress$new()
    progress$set(message = "Data Import", value = 0)
    # Close the progress when this reactive exits (even if there's an error)
    on.exit(progress$close())
    # Create a callback function to update progress.
    # Each time this is called:
    # - If `value` is NULL, it will move the progress bar 1/(5*2) of the remaining
    #   distance. If non-NULL, it will set the progress to that value.
    # - It also accepts optional detail text.
    updateProgress <- function(value = NULL, detail = NULL) {
      if (is.null(value)) {
        value <- progress$getValue()
        value <- value + (progress$getMax() - value) / (5 * 2)
      }
      progress$set(value = value, detail = detail)

The eventReactiveAsync() function is very short in my gist, so you should be able to adapt it quickly to your needs. Although I think you can use it out of the box without modifications as well.

The setup is fairly simple (and not too original): 
  1. start a 'multiprocess' future (i.e. on *nix based system do a fork of the process, on Windows start a new process). The future package will export the relevant objects to the new process by examining the handler expression.
  2. set up an observer that checks if the results are ready via 'future::resolved()' (note the 'd' at the end, this is a non-blocking check) 
  3. if results are ready invalidate with the calculated value the reactive that is produced by the eventReactiveAsync() function.
I am not sure what the advantage is of the 'callr' package mentioned by Dean compared to 'future', as it also starts a new R process. What is nice about 'future' on the other hand is the automatic variable exporting based on the expression to be evaluated.

Cheers,

Andras

On Sunday, 11 June 2017 06:58:12 UTC-4, Andrew Sali wrote:
Hi Shiny Users,

I was recently wondering about the potential approaches to circumvent the synchronous nature of R / Shiny, in particular that a long-running R calculation will block the whole user interface. My first intuition is that spawning separate R processes is the only way to go. 

Using the 'future' package I have come up with an asynchronous drop-in replacement to eventReactive, which requires no code change compared to the usual eventReactive and can achieve asynchronous (non-blocking) evaluation. A small gist is available here: https://gist.github.com/andrewsali/3317e5954459fef2f5fed68d68c1ac92 

The reason for using the 'future' package is that it takes care of spawning the new R process and automatically exporting the relevant variables by static code inspection of the handler expression.

However this approach also has a few small drawbacks: 1) it's not possible to have side-effects in the handler expression, 2) The reactive produced by my async version will not invalidate downstream when the calculation starts, but instead when the calculation finishes and the value is returned. This means that the 'recalculating' class (opacity) is not applied to an output depending on the async reactive whilst the calculation is running.

The reason why I thought to make eventReactive async is that the event expression (usually the fast part) can remain synchronous and the long-running handler expression can be sent for async evaluation. Also, by creating an async version of a 'reactive' it's relatively a minor issue that side-effects are not allowed for in the handler expression.

I would be very curious to know what others have been doing to have async / non-blocking behaviour in Shiny. Also, as far as I know there is an 'async' version of Shiny being worked on, I would be interested if there is some information on what the underlying approach taken is.

Cheers,

Andras
